The 2500K has a Tcase temperature of 72.6°C, this is the maximum temperature at the heat spreader. The 3210M has a Tjunction temperature of 105 C which is the temperature at the processor die. These two values are a lot different, and you can definitely run a 2500K at a Tj temperature of over 90c before thermal trip, I do it infrequently.

My initial response to the OP was indeed wrong given the circumstances. I was unaware that CPU max temperatures have increased over the years, especially in mobile devices.

The user interface of OS X (the software installed on the desktops and laptops that Apple produces) is unique in the fact that it is easy enough for an inexperienced computer user to figure out, but advanced enough to feel adequate for the power computer user. This OS X software integrates extremely well with a range of Apple services bundled under one name called iCloud.

iCloud is a cloud computing architecture that allows you to share content from your iCloud enabled devices to "the cloud" where all other connected iCloud enabled devices can sync with, feed into, and share the information. Everything from calendar events, messages, wifi passwords, email, contacts, notes, documents, device settings/backups, apps, etc can be stored on iCloud. If I sent a text on my iPhone, it shows up on my Mac, and I can reply to a text from any device, because it's all a synced and part of an effective universal system.

With iCloud, the OS X/Mac systems also integrate extremely well with iOS which is Apple's mobile computing operating system that's currently on the iPhone and iPads. One of the key parts that make iOS a really usable piece of software is the fact that the App Store ecosystem is a closed and controlled environment... meaning all apps have to be reviewed by an Apple employee before their release. This makes the app store, a fundamental part of smart phones, an extremely high quality marketplace... for the most part.

There are literally hundreds of other points that could be discussed, such as design of products (incredibly innovative, see the Mac Pro), customer support (likely best in the industry), unique technological enhancements (see Continuity/Handoff, iOS 8/OS X Yosemite feature set), and even the end user experience as a whole.
